wa_vanishing_point.notes: Starts just left of the prominent arete dividing Dolomite Tower; the first two bolts are visible from the ground. Pull left under a small overhang straight off the ground, then follow bolts up and left and back right around the arete. Graded 5.10 to 5.10c. Often linked with pitch 2.

Straight up, then trend left on bolts, turn the corner and pull back onto the arete to a bolted stance on a pedestal. Optional finger-sized gear, or a hand crack to the right at 5.10a. A 60 m rope barely links pitches 1 and 2.

Scramble up a ledge, clip a bolt and traverse right onto a pedestal of stacked blocks, then climb the corner on three bolts and gear. Before the 2020 bolt additions this pitch was runout and loose. Ends on a good ledge.

Steep finger and thin-hand crack in the corner beside a crystalline face, with the hardest moves just above the anchor. The main gear pitch. Belay on a ledge out left about 25 ft below the roof; do not climb past it.

Up steep blocks and left onto a face with three bolts, then jog right on two more; do not head out to the arete. A large part of the original roof has fallen away. Parties who climbed the older line felt it far harder than its 5.11c grade.

Step down and right off the belay, then follow roughly 10–12 bolts through a band of poor rock, with a 5.11c section near the top on the arete. Test holds; the bolting is close enough that a broken hold is not a disaster.
Steep arete climbing just left of the prow, with a thin, hard sequence close to the belay and tricky moves above. A small piece protects the final moves. Some parties rate the key move 5.12+.

Three bolts of 5.11 on the arete, then veer left into a slabby, shallow dihedral with a bolt on the arete. The most serious pitch on the route: the upper section has runouts of about 25 ft on 5.7–5.9 ground. Bring small and medium nuts.
One of the two best pitches: a crimpy boulder problem on the arete, a rest at deep pockets, then a second hard boulder. Bring every draw.
Past four bolts in lichen-covered rock to the old death-flake anchor, then clip the bolt above the roof and traverse right on jugs. The 2020 reroute avoids the loose death flake entirely.
Pull back left out the roof on big jugs to a hard boulder problem on the vertical headwall, just out of sight from the belay. Short, all bolts, and the likely crux of the route (5.12b).
Pockets and crimps up steep ground, then back right to the arete and a belay perched on the prow. All bolts. It can be linked with pitch 11 to avoid the poor intermediate belay.
Straight up past a bolt onto ledgy climbing, with gear and one or two more bolts, to chains on a slab.

Two bolts up a dirty slab to a juggy hand crack, over a bolted roof, then slab to a two-bolt anchor right at the lip and the edge of the woods. Scramble down heather to pick up the base-jumper descent trail.

wa_primal_scream.notes: Pull over or around the short wall capped by a 3 in horizontal crack, then follow low humped ridges to two diagonal cracks. Pass a cedar bush on its left to blocks in a right-facing corner. A bolt protects the step left onto knobs and a dirt pedestal. From its top, step down and left across a deep cleft to big cracks and knobs to the anchor.

A clean slab on small edges past a bolt leads to an exfoliation crack. Most of the pitch is a long undercling up a grassy, dirt-filled 1 in crack whose gardened slots take gear well; doubles from 0.75 to 2 in are useful. Near the top, step right on edges over two small overlaps to the anchor.
Keep underclinging along the seams between granite layers, friction for the feet, past one bolt. A second bolt near the top protects the move over an overlap, which goes on good knobs.

Up a shallow groove where protection is hard to find, taking the best rock on the right of a large tree patch. Cross left above the trees, where the rock turns crumbly on the pull onto a broad, lower-angled ledge. Scramble diagonally left to the anchor on the very edge of the buttress crest.
Angle right across a stretch of blank rock to a set of narrow dihedrals, then climb into a slot between two exfoliating sheets of granite.
A jagged finger crack with good gear starts the pitch. It then hugs the right side of a tree patch before easing onto lower-angle knobs and smears.
Unremarkable ground up blocks, tilted ramps and lichen-covered slabs. Stay on the cleanest rock; the overlaps to either side are heavily lichened.
More moderate face climbing, on noticeably cleaner rock than the pitch below.

Head for an S-shaped crack that takes gear but narrows below finger width. A bulge above goes right on smearing moves. Blocks and flakes then lead to the chains on the ridge top, the same anchor that tops pitch 11 of Concerto in C for Drill and Hammer.

From here the route follows the ridge to the summit alongside Concerto in C for Drill and Hammer's pitches 12-14. Keep to good rock on the ridge's right margin rather than thrashing through the brush on top. Climb blocky, ledgy ground up the right side of the crest to a chain anchor on the crest. Bolts are sparse on the ridge.
Scramble up the ridge until trees push you right, then step down onto the slab layer just below them. Follow its dihedral, which protects well, to a chain anchor on a small stance.

Step right past an obvious clean 3 in crack and around the bulge up and right. Climb a rib with a horizontal slot for a small piece, then a bolt, and pass some bushes to a white rib with a second bolt. Keep left of a tree and push through its branches into wide cracks between blocks, reaching the chain anchor on the summit.

wa_spectre_peak_south_route.notes: Start up right of the entry notch: about 100 ft of 4th-class scrambling leads into 100 ft of 5.7 climbing up blocky terrain; some parties simul-climb this pitch to the first ledge.
Continue up low-fifth-class blocky ground to a large, tree-dotted ledge, then traverse left to gain the ridge crest proper.

The technical crux: climbs the cleaner face right of a prominent mossy gully, where roughly 10 ft of overhanging, chossy rock adds spice above sparse protection; the parallel gully itself offers a looser but more protectable fallback line.
Solid cracks and ledgy slabs lead up toward the crest on noticeably better rock than the pitches below.
Clean-walled climbing along a narrow, exposed knife-edge stretch of the ridge crest.
Continued crest climbing on generally solid gneiss to a stance below the ridge's gendarme band.

Follow the crest past a funky notch to the base of an imposing, shattered gendarme where the rock is sharp and loose enough to 'sing' when tapped; a roughly 25m rappel into the gap is followed by a self-belayed ascent of the far wall.
The route's best pitch: a clean 20-30 ft hands-and-fists crack gives genuinely fun, well-protected climbing to a belay alcove.
Steep, featured face climbing with abundant gear placements on solid rock.
Easier ground over heather ramps and blocky terrain, working back toward the ridge crest.
Traverse just below the crest for about 100 ft of low-fifth-class terrain on loose, gravel-covered rock -- careful footwork required.

Final technical pitch weaves through narrow, hoodoo-like towers of soft, chalky rock reminiscent of Utah's Fisher Towers; top out with a ~30m rappel from the last tower to a big grassy ledge, then simul-climb roughly 600 ft of 3rd/4th-class terrain (with a couple of low-5th moves, roughly 5.0) to the summit.
